chapter: Jelly Roll, Leonard Reed and Chicago mixed crowds
title: White musicians sitting in in New Orleans
summary: He recalls a white trumpet learner and boy Joe Gondolfi who got him dances.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Did they have mixed bands down here when you were playing in the twenties?
You didn't know? I didn't remember that.
You don't remember any white boys that ever sat in with you and anything? Well, yeah.

They had a boy named Jogan Duffy. Well, he couldn't play that, you know, but he would learn how to play trumpets. You know, I'd make him sit right side of me in the band and play along with me and dance and things, you know. But Joe never did learn I don't think. I haven't seen him since I left, since I've been back. I know he's an old man like I am now. See I was so good with him because he'd follow us everywhere, everywhere we went. Joe would go and his dad had a big market out there on Chippewa and something out there in front of town. And I never had to worry about no, you know, meats and things. I would go out there and get my meats and things, the time I got ready. That boy was crazy about me and I liked him. Joe Gondolfi, I never would get him.
Many other guys like that, did you remember all of them?
He's about the only one I remember. Goldeir has a lot more of them, but.
He's the only one whose name you can remember.
And he'd go around and get up dances for me. At the Italian Hall and Espinade and Ramport. All the dances I played there he got them for me.
